text: Great message. One thing you forgot and that is a big deal, at least based on my experience, is the feeling of being broken down the next morning. After every rolling-intensive training, you will be waking up in a significant pain that is pulsating throughout your whole body. text:
Great video! I've been rolling bjj for 3 months now. I'm located at a great gym with a great culture, with the head coach from America. Unfortunately, I got ringworm after a few weeks of training. I took my hygiene seriously, but I have started to shower at my gym to prevent catching staff/ringworm ect.

What I took away from this video / linking to my own training: 

1. Ego does exist. I remember rolling with someone who was rolling at 100% intensity, and this was not fun. All they want to do is beat you and at the end of the round walk off, as a white belt it is much better to do 'positional sparring' instead of trying to take someone's head off. 

2. This links to 1, if you are drilling / sparring it is much better to tap early to prevent a broken bone / hyperextended joint. In a comp... sure.. a bit different. 

But anyways... if you are a 0 stripe white belt like me, I believe it is more valuable to positional spar to learn techniques, than go 100% and try completely choke out your partner every single time.



I thought this video had many valuable points. Keep it up.

text:
Interesting take on the sport and awesome work having a year under your belt is awesome. 

I'd like to add to the conversation about injuries. One of the best things you can do to reduce your risk of injuries is to do some form of S&C work off the mats (the more 'BJJ specific' the better). Studies show that by doing S&C you reduce your risk of acute injury by 30% and overuse injuries by 50% which is huge. 

As far as steroids are concerned, I think that this is an issue for high-level competitors but will be essentially a non-factor for the everyday hobbyist and something that shouldn't really be dwelled on for most people IMO. I personally am against PED usage in BJJ completely, and I think as a community we have the power to impact change in the long term if it's something we are collectively against.

Combative sports require a certain capacity for strength, flexibility, hard work, pain, humility, technical savvy and mental resilience. text:
Judo/jiu jitsu weren’t made for smaller people, it was developed by the samurai to engage another armed samurai after they lost their weapon. Kano adapted for use without armor once the samurai era ended. Helio was 6’4 and couldn’t get the leverage for the throws, so he focused mostly on the ground, that’s how BJJ was born.

Jiu jitsu is like any other martial art and sport, when skill is near equal, athletic attributes matter. Jiu jitsu will work against almost any person regardless of size and strength, if they are untrained. Choose your sparring partners wisely

text:
After training Jiu Jitsu for 6 months, I can say with certainty that it’s much more dangerous than most people make it seem, and that’s sad IMO. I used to play basketball through college, and had various small injuries doing that (ankle sprains, hamstring pulls, even a couple of minor surgeries). 

It’s nothing like BJJ. It’s rare to go even two weeks of training without sustaining some kind of small nagging injury, best-case. Every sparring session, you can get judo thrown and fall directly on your shoulder getting it hurt or dislocated, get your ankles twisted badly when getting swept (when on top), hurt your lower back when getting stacked (on bottom), etc. I say this as a guy who religiously does yoga and weight training in addition to BJJ, and goes the extra mile on nutrition and recovery. It’s a combat sport and you’re going to get hurt - a lot. It’s a beautiful game, but I’ve had my doubts about continuing due to the injuries.
video_title: Is BJJ Worth All Injuries ?

text: From my Judo instructor of 70 years experience: you have to do it lightly to moderately capacity, and practice it with lighter weight and advanced and experienced people. This lessens you're chances of injury. Avoid competition. In Judo, we also have a world of rules learned empirically that do not exist in Jiu-Jitsu, so we're lightyears ahead in that respect. text: This question was asked to the wrong guy. You need to ask a guy in his late 40's, 50's or older. In my 50's now and I can say that I had a great time training in martial arts (judo, karate, jiujitsu, boxing and MMA). In my 40's I realized I was having problems, too much wear and tear on the body (mostly my neck and shoulders but also my hands and knees). Eventually I made the decision to stop training as the injuries were coming more frequently and taking much longer to heal, while at the same time I was slowing down with reflex time. Now, I miss training. There is nothing like training and going toe to toe with someone, testing yourself in so many ways. Having also worked in security and law enforcement on two continents, I can also say that having martial arts knowledge did save me from at least getting seriously injured more than once in real world situations. All of this said, was it worth it? Probably not. That doesn't stop me from feeling this void of not rolling these days. I think the advice I'd give someone is to train, but to train in moderation. We don't all need to aspire to UFC potential (unless that's what you're going for). Realize that training should be a lifelong pursuit and take your time. Supplement your training with flexibility and resistance training so that you are physically fit, well balanced and after a few years of practice also skilled with martial arts. Be smart about how you train, train for the long haul not the short term gains. This way, you will have less injuries and be able to enjoy the activity a lot longer.

I don't care about my flexibility anymore.  For me, I wear knee braces, ankle and elbow braces, and I take 45 mins before class to properly stretch and tape my fingers and toes. text: White belt here. I literally just quit BJJ after 12 months. In and out of training because of injuries. I got two neck injuries, rib injury, finger and wrist. all minor but stops me from other activities like mtb, triathlon training, soccer. Too many aggressive partners. Im 6ft1 210# and decent shape so new partners think I'm gonna use strength and go hard against me. I use less than half strength and focus on good movement and technique. But their first flurry of attacks before I mount them or take their back is injuring me. I take 4 BJJ classes per week but when I get injured I have to stop the other dozen activities I do per week which is very irritating. So I canceled my membership and setup my basement with mats, grappling dummy and heavy bag. I will drill for a few months daily at home until my movement and submission tools are two levels better then return to class as much better grappler. There are times in rolling where I didnt have a move in certain positions so I was smashed until I got to a position I had moves in. When I return I will have at least 5 moves in all positions so that I can better protect myself. Movements, sweeps, submissions, escapes. I know not rolling with a person is less effective but I can get alot more reps at home than in class. in class you take turns practicing a move with a partner. Maybe you get 50 reps in an hour. At home I can rep the move 500 times with a dummy in that same time. Literally 10x the reps. Then when I return to class any partner is gonna have a seriously hard time putting me in a bad position when my training accumulation is 5-10 times higher than them.

BJJ is so much *less* dangerous than other grappling sports, though. It's slower paced (especially with the gi), and you don't get the dynamic power moves of judo or wrestling. text: I'm aware that most injuries are unlucky accidents incurred while rolling, and not a result of not tapping in time like one would think at first, and imo, it's largely preventable by not rolling so hard. In 9 years of doing jujutsu, I've not gotten seriously injured (as in, had an injury that put me out of training for more than a week) and I've only seriously injured a partner once. Sure, I train a lot less than others, but that one time was when my partner and I were both going unneccessarily hard and we've learnt our lesson right then and there. Had we continued going hard every time, it would have been much more injurious. Recently, I've been training with a guy from another dojo that's more BJJ-focused and the increase in close calls on my part is very noticeable. And I hate it. I just want to have fun, learn and go home uninjured, sometimes I have work right after training and when I don't, my boss still relies on me for the next day and I just hate getting injured as well. And what were these close calls caused by? Going hard, i.e. pulling joint locks fast. Trying to execute dangerous moves, especially takedowns targeting the knees with a sideways motion or turning me around on the ground by rapidly applying an arm lock targeting the shoulder. Not trusting me not to hurt him, and applying painful and at times dangerous counters to stop me from what I wasn't intending on doing in the first place. Did any of those situations need to be as dangerous as they were? Nope. And especially the last one, this culture of not trusting, is not something I want to see poisoning the dojo I train at. We all go onto the mat knowing that the other person cares about our wellbeing and this trust is what enables learning because fighting or hard rolling is not where you learn the best. Your brain is in an adrenaline-filled response, unable to think clearly. It surely is beneficial to put your brain into such a situation every once in a while, but for regular training, going slow and allowing your partner to do stuff and learn is best.

text: I'm 48.  I'm an athlete.  I've been doing bjj since 1998 and I'm still running through gyms submitting everyone, including the coaches.  And after almost 30 years I still don't really have any injuries.  The biggest thing I notice with BJJ vs almost all other sports is that most other sports have real athletes because you get weeded out when you're not.  Most bjj practitioners are NOT athletes.  Like at ALL.  I have to go like 30% almost all of the time.  They are just regular people with regular genetics and if they had tried to wrestle (for example) they would not have made the team and therefore would not have been wrestling for a long time.  But with BJJ you literally just sign up and you're in.  Most of the "athletes" in your average BJJ room (even world champions) are accountants, baristas and Walmart managers with totally average or below average genetics.  The harsh reality is most people arent athletes, and your bodies will break to varying degrees trying to do athletic things.  Just look at BJJ's average philosophy on training takedowns?  They dont do it.  Why?  We dont want people to get hurt?  So they butt scoot all over the place.  Meanwhile every olympic level judoka or wrestler has been doing non-stop, brutal takedowns since they were 5. text:
What Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, as a still quite young martial art, clearly seems to be missing is more guidance for practitioners on how to properly warm up, roll safely and how to cool down and "rearrange" your body/get tenions out at the end of a class.

The warm ups are mediocre at best in most places I saw or heard of a systematic cool down as part of the curriculum is pretty much non existent. There is no widespread systematic approach on getting people to learn how to spar slowly (conscious breathing f.e.) from the get go, instead a lot of people start ripping on their joints and trying to break each others bones from lesson one with full force at full speed. What the hell do people think is gonna happen? 

It's a shame actually, because theoretically is a great, great tool to learn about yourself, life as such, to stay fit, creative and much more. The way most classes are being run now, with the 0 - 10 or maybe 15 minutes warm ups and no cool downs in most classes, it is doomed to cause a tremendous amount of injuries, especially looking at how the overall health of the average person has declined over the last decades. The younger generations will get injured even sooner and more severely because of how physically unfit most of them are. We need to adress this as a community. It's far more important than any new technique on how to break something. We need to invest much more time in learning how to maintain health.

text:
Is BJJ Worth All Injuries? No—unless you’re a professional athlete or an MMA fighter. If your goal is to train for fun, maintain longevity, and stay in good shape, it doesn’t make sense to risk serious injuries like torn ligaments or damage to your neck. I’ve trained in boxing, Muay Thai, Sambo, and BJJ, and I can say BJJ tends to be far more traumatic. The injuries go beyond simple bruises and can be worse than those in striking martial arts. My own BJJ training schedule often looked like one week on, followed by two weeks of recovery, then starting over.
BJJ is certainly a practical and efficient martial art, but if you want athletic longevity, it might not be the best choice.

I’ve been in the Army for 12 years, and anyone who has served that long knows motivation can fade over time.

 About two years ago I started training Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, and it has honestly changed my life. I went from a white belt to a blue belt with a stripe, and the impact has been incredible.

When you combine Jiu Jitsu with weight training, it creates a level of conditioning that makes you feel unstoppable.

But the biggest change hasn’t just been physical. Training has given me a renewed drive in every area of my life. It’s pushed me to do better at my job, stay focused in college, and be a better father and husband. It brought back a level of discipline and motivation that I didn’t realize I was missing.

It’s also had a huge impact on my physical fitness in the Army. I almost maxed my last ACFT, and it felt incredible to see that progress pay off.

With the help of God and Jiu Jitsu, my life has genuinely improved in ways I didn’t expect. It gave me purpose, structure, and the motivation to keep pushing myself every day.

text:
I trained BJJ for over a year before I joined the USMC and earned a Blue Belt. The Marines have something called MCMAP (Marine Corps Martial Arts Program). Out of boot camp all Marines earn a Tan Belt (entry level belt). When I got to my first unit the MCMAP instructor was a Brown Belt. He was blown away that I was able to land 'advanced techniques' like triangle chokes, keylocks, and armbar variations. His head exploeded the first time I pulled Rubber Guard (Eddie Bravo had recently gained a lot of popularity and had published his Jiu Jitsu Unleashed book). They acted like I was some kind of grappling prodigy. I wasn't, I was just an average Blue Belt at my local BJJ gym. I was pretty shocked to see how little some of the more advanced MCMAP techniques were things I saw kids learning in BJJ classes. 

When I got my Black Belt in MCMAP, the instructors routinely would ask me for tips on how to use techniques in different situations. I would end up helping teach the classes and it actually had an impact on many of my fellow students. I loved when I had wrestlers working with me. We would feed off of each other on the mats and I think we all ended up elevating our game. By the time I was in class to get my Black Belt I had become much more familiar with my Rubber Guard and was usually trying to work on those techniques. I remember throwing an Oma Plata one day and the entire class stopped and it convinced several people to start training BJJ on the side. 

My son (age 9) recently started training and after his first day of classes told me that he can't wait to learn more!

text: There's a difference between self-defense jiu-jitsu and sport jiu-jitsu. The problem nowadays is so many schools are just teaching the sport variety which operates under a certain rule set and helps you win grappling competitions. Berimbolos and a lot of leg locks carry little transfer to self defense situations. But traditional jiu-jitsu consisting of good clinch work, trips, judo throws, elbows, knees and leg kicks as well as how to control the distance and how to stand up after being knocked or taken down are invaluable. They've saved me many times. Find a good school and never forget why you signed up for class in the first place. I bet it was to learn self-defense... not win tournaments. Oss!

text:
Most fights people have in mind are bar fights where someone’s ego is talking shit and then it escalates. These are precisely the easiest fights to avoid and you should because more than likely he has friends that are drunk and rowdy. 

However, you can avoid those situations by not going out to the bar to begin with or just not chirping back when they are talking drunk smack. 


But let’s say you end up in an altercation outside the bar environment anyway, any martial art will be fine as long as you are proficient. The problem with a striking art is that it takes a much longer time to be so good that the average guy stands zero chance, anyone can get a lucky punch in. However, if someone is an elite wrestler or skilled in BJJ against an untrained person there is almost zero chance untrained guy wins. Plus you avoid breaking their face and getting sued. In grappling you also experience live sparring every single day in practice at full speed so you are actually fighting on a daily basis which is far better preparation. But I still think knowing both a striking and grappling art is essential.

text: For me - basics of boxing, basics of BJJ, basics of MMA, basics of some "good" Krav Maga (situational awareness, defense to multiple opponents, using "forbidden" hits, surrounding items..). It is unlikely that some experienced martial artist or MMA guy would start a fight first. Thatswhy basics should be enough. Real life (not mine) experience: some guy on drugs entered narrow corridor in the house. Houseowner started punching him, kicking to groins etc. - nothing, guy was so high he couldn't feel the pain. So options left - either put him to sleep (if possible) or : start hitting collar bone, once broken (easily), arms not usable. kicking the knee from the side - again , once dislocated, attacker can not move. I know it is quite rough, but if one is in such situation protecting close ones, then it is good strategy. Injuries will heal, no damage to spine, head etc., you even would stand trial in case of need. And such scenarios should all good "self defense systems" teach.

I disagree. JiuJitsu is very useful, especially against multiple people. You should try running if threatened by more than one person and most of the times the only reason you were unable to do so is if one of them grabs you. Breaking grips and/or your opponents control over your body is a very big part of JiuJitsu.

Furthermore sometimes you will want to restrain people without risking permanently damaging them, I.e. if the drunk uncle on your family gathering gets aggressive or something like that. 

Grappling has it‘s place and can be very useful, just like striking. It depends on the situation really but generally I‘d say it‘s 50/50 and just train what you feel more comfortable in

The greatest benefit of Jiu Jitsu isn't self defense or fitness; it's a mirror. It shows you everything you lack while in a high pressure situation.

If you're physically weak, it will show you that.
If your stamina sucks, it will show you that.
If you panic under pressure, it will show you that. It will reveal you to yourself and you can't run from the truth because it was shown to you in the context of combat.

But the inverse is also true. It will show you all your strengths. I was lucky in that it proved to me that i really was all the things i believed myself to be.

text: Didn't realize Chewy was a cat guy. Much respect. Much love for your poor little kitten. I'm sure he's had a good life and was loved. With regard to the topic, I don't love bjj. I'm a purple belt, and I initially enrolled for the self-defense aspect. I saw Royler Gracie in those Gracie In Action videos, and I thought a little guy like him who was mopping the floor with everyone was absolutely stunning. Over 6 years later, I like bjj less and less as each day passes because it's become so different from the original Gracie Jiu-Jitsu that had originally captivated me. The sportive aspect of bjj is what really ruins your body, and I'm just not interested in bjj as a sport. If you're at a sport school, if you can tweak it to meet your original goals of being able to defend yourself, then I think it's worth it. If all you're learning is spider guard, inversions, and pulling guard, I would say it's definitely not worth it. Ruining your body and not being a legit martial artist would not be worth it.

I agree. I think the caveat to this is what do you want out of BJJ as an individual? Not everyone is going to have the same goals. Some want to compete and roll every other day while others just want to train a few times a week to stay healthy and learn to improve technique. 

I fall into the latter category. I’m 52 years old and the smallest guy in the gym. Been training for 4 years now and have had good and bad days. I love it but I hate it too. Sounds contradictory but it’s true. I hate it because when I wrestled as a young boy into my late teens, there were too many expectations and I can empathize about having thoughts of doubts “if this is for me”. I have to tell myself that BJJ is a hobby and not a chore (like scholastic wrestling was). It’s the reason why I love it too. No expectations and just show up. 🤙

text:
The first time I was invited to train jiu jitsu I was 21 or 22. I absolutely loved it and was consistent for 6ish months and even did a local comp 12 weeks in. I did horrible but it was awesome 😂 After that, I didn’t train again for over a year. And that was the beginning of a cycle that perpetuated for years. 1-3 months on, a year off. On repeat.  

Fast forward to now, I’m 32, married with 2 kids and the guys that originally invited me are all black belts and brown belts. 

For the last 5/6 months, I’ve gotten real serious about making bjj more of a lifestyle routine. Just a week ago I competed in my first no-gi comp. I didn’t win that one either but I certainly did a lot better this time 🤣

If there’s anything I regret about my journey so  far, it’s that I didn’t stick with it 10 years ago. Not because of the belts. But because of the lack of progress as a man that I missed out on from not making it a financial or physical priority. I got fat, I became stagnant, I got lazy. I literally couldn’t carry my kids upstairs without getting winded.  All because I made excuses to not train or take care of myself. Look, I get it. I’ve got a job, wife, 2 toddlers and a mortgage to pay. We’re all busy. I only train 2 times a week on average. Occasionally I’ll get to a 3rd practice, but that’s rare. Do what you can and commit to what’s reasonable within the non-negotiables of your schedule. 
 
Of course the physical perks of getting in shape are awesome. And training is a ton of fun. But the best part of all, it’s helping me be a better father and husband by instilling discipline and focus in my daily routine that didn’t exist before.

And look, I don’t want to make the sport seem like it’s something it’s not, but it truly has given me a confidence and drive that I had lost years ago.  I can carry my kids up a flight of stairs without losing my breath. I can rough house with them and throw them across the couch almost endlessly 😂 I have more clarity. My stress levels have dramatically lessened. I feel regulated emotionally. And this clarity has allowed me to be more present, focused and supportive of my wife on a daily basis. 

It hasn’t been this crazy spiritual revelation that some people often try to make it. Get to a local church and read the bible for that. But the mental clarity and physical improvements have been life changing for my family. 

This has turned into a novel. Didn’t intend to do that, haha. As I listened to the video, I felt compelled to share the journey I’ve been on in hopes that someone who may be in a similar spot would see this and be encouraged to commit to training something. Make the commitment. Even if it’s not bjj. Maybe it’s running or weight lifting. It doesn’t matter. At some point you will look back and you will regret not making the commitment. God Bless ✌️

text:
I’d put it slightly differently. It may be worth doing anyway, but if you don’t enjoy it you ain’t gonna. But the fact that you didn’t love it as a kid don’t mean you’re sure to hate it as an adult. You were a child and thought as children think.

Here’s what I think might have been going on. You weren’t a naturally athletic kid. Strong, fast, coordinated, those kind of things. So as a beginner, you double sucked, from a combination of physical and skill reasons. And, also as a kid, you needed to be good to feel validated and enjoy the thing. Instead you got non-stop demonstrations of being not good , or not as as good as the other kids.

But you’re older now. It’s possible that you could go to a bjj club and enjoy the process of learning, instead of chasing the validation of “being awesome”. As an adult you might see that pretty much everyone who comes to bjj suck at it for a long time. Accepting failure and learning from it is central to the art. Accepting that there are people whom you can beat easily (very few at first), people on about your level, and people who are so far beyond you that you can’t even imagine giving them a challenging roll. That’s an important aspect of bjj. But you don’t need to compete with them, in fact, you shouldn’t. The person you’re trying to beat is yourself from last month.

I’m 54. I’ve been doing this for less than two years. There are old blackbelts whom I will never catch up with, in the decades I have left. There are 25-year-olds with competition ready bodies who could fold me in half even if they wasn’t five or ten years ahead of me in skill. But myself from last spring… I’d smash that guy.

So give it a try. You might find that some things that felt intolerable to you then are insignificant now. You might find things to love that you were blind to back then. They are there.

Cheers

text: Ju Jitsu is great. For strictly one on one, organized, regulated, sport. But it falls apart in real life situations. Where ones actual LIFE, is on the line.  Their are no rules, banned strikes, point deductions, or disqualification, in street fights, survival situations. 9 times out of 10, survival situations, street fights, involve multiple attackers, and deadly, deadly weapons. And you will get zero cooperation from your attackers, if you say "time out, can't you see my entire body is preoccupied with this rear naked choke? Stand by please, until I'm done ankle locking or choking out your buddy." You are going to get soccer kicked in the face, stomped by another attacker/multiple attackers, stabbed, or hit with an object. I think ju jitsu is awesome to learn. But, I think most people get the false impression that its the most effective fighting style ever created. Because it works incredibly well in the UFC.

text: I trained for years and we would have “open mat challenges” for random people off the street to challenge any blue belt or higher rank they wished in any style of fighting they wanted for three months of jiujitsu for free. If they took down or submitted any bluebor higher training is on us for three months. Needless to say no one was ever able to submit or takedown anyone the rank of blue or higher when they challenged. The point we were trying to make was a) you’re either a trained fighter or you are not and you’re not able to take down anyone who is actually trained and b) THAT is how effective jiu jitsu is. Of the people that came to open matt sessions that were submitted handover fist they joined our gym. Thats how we recruited people. most people that came to the gym wanted to legitimately see how effective jujutsu was and to possibly join. Two guys that I’m aware of came because they thought they were actually tough. Their attitude and the way they acted walking in that gym dictated that they went to sleep on those two instances. Those were the only two people we ever put to sleep intentionally.

text: What people forget in situations like that is how little control anyone actually has once a fight starts. You never know who in the crowd might jump in, who might have a knife, or what the other person might be hiding under their clothes. Even a skilled jiu-jitsu fighter who locks in a clean choke is gambling with blind spots and timing he can’t manage on the ground. Real martial discipline isn’t about taking someone down; it’s about reading the danger, keeping distance, and staying out of range of hidden variables that can end a fight in seconds for all the wrong reasons.

text:
My kids learn Muay Thai and western boxing for striking, wrestling and jiujitsu for ground confidence, and judo for transitioning between the two. We don’t emphasize anything high level. Just master four basic principles of each martial art. I really mean master it. 
Must Thai: perfect punch, elbow, knee, and kicking technique.
Wrestling/Jiujitsu: chokes, arm/leg locks/bars, take down offense and defense. 
Judo: four basic throws. 
It’s for self defense not competition in our house. 
If they want to compete they can lick a discipline and go for it, but regardless everyone has to MASTER those basic things in those specific disciplines. 
I subscribe to the idea that I’d more fear the person that has practiced a single move a thousand times, than a hundred moves one time.
I enjoy judo the best at my age now. When I was younger I preferred striking.

text:
Love your show Joe Rogan. I liked it when you said " find a bjj school with good ethics." I've done martial arts ever since I was a kid, had a few fights with bigger kids (much bigger kids). My first fight was in the school bathroom. I was in first grade, the boy was in 7th grade at the time. My second fight was at the school hall. Again, I was in first grade and both my opponents were in 7th grade. The last fight I had was at a park, I can't even remember how many boys I was fighting at the same time. My father trained Chinese Kung Fu when he was a boy. My father tought me one of the most important lessons of Kung Fu "Never tell anyone that you know Kung Fu" my father said. "Kung Fu is not to show off, you can only use Kung Fu when there is no other choice". The reason for this comment is because I joined a few BJJ classes, and I was DISGUSTED with the lack of morals in the classes. The skills of BJJ are good enough to take a man's life away. Without the proper education of ethics and selfcontrol BJJ students will know how to suffocate someone to death, but won't have a clue on how to de-escalate a situation. You have a great show Joe Rogan, it would be great if you could make a video of the importance of ethics being tought in every BJJ school in the country. I know that now in day in America we have the culture of being a BAD BOY or a BEAST. And if someone wants to be a BEAST,  at least be a BEAST with strong ethics and morals. 
At the end of the day the best Martial art is Social Intelligence.

I wrestled in high school and was decent at it.  When I went up against the guys who would go on to place in state championships later, however, it was rough.  The stuff Rogan says here about "I'm screwed" in ground game apparently translates.  If someone is better than you by enough, there is not much you can do.  People with no ground experience are instantly done if they get trapped there, but even a sufficient skill/strength gap does the job.

In the matches, I could hold those guys off from pinning me and narrow the margin of defeat, so the opposing team received fewer points for their win.  In an actual fight, they could just pick whatever they wanted that would allow them to hit me without me being able to hit back.  That wasn't lost on me, even back then.

text:
Started BJJ in November. I haven't full rolled yet, other than little spurts while practicing techniques. My partner is also a white belt. One day our normal prof wasn't there so a brown belt taught the class. 

We asked him for help on a technique that was just passing guard into side control (I'm horrible with the names). So he did the technique on me, and the difference in pressure/weight/uncomfort with how he did it vs how me and my partner were doing it was unreal. I mean it was a quick pass, but it was like he had so much weight that just transitioned from my leg, up through my hip, to my midsection making it hard to breath.

Joe's line about how most people have no idea how defenseless they'd be if a BJJ black belt grabbed ahold of them makes me think of that small exchange. If you just watched it, you'd see nothing different, but BJJ is so deep. It's "simple" sure, "you grab this sleeve, this collar, foot here, pull/twist and now you're on top"... but there's so many small things with weight, momentum, the grip you make when you grab, shifting weight a little bit here at this moment, etc and it just completely changes how effective/smooth it feels. It's nuts. And addictive.

text:
People from other arts endlessly malign the BJJ guard, and while it obviously is not a very practical or recommendable strategy to pull guard in MMA or self defense the majority of the time, it is still well within the realm of possibility that you will trip and fall, be taken down, be attacked while sitting down, or countless other such scenarios. A lot of the time, standing up may be a superior option to entering a confrontation on those terms, but that is not guaranteed to be either possible or ideal. 
 For this reason, I think it is good that despite the stigma, there are people in BJJ who spend so much time developing and exhibiting strategies which begin from open guard. It is not a comprehensive self-preservation strategy, but it's usefulness as a skill depends as much on the circumstances of the confrontation as it does with striking, wrestling, running, shooting or parkour.

text:
I came to BJJ at 29 y.o. With almost no previous experience in martial art. I've never been in a fight since high school, and I never been good at any of them either. I really don't know how to act in fights.

But eventually I started BJJ, and I see many debates on it's effectiveness, comparing to Boxing or other standing martial arts. And most of the people talking about it in the extremes. But for average people like myself... whether it BJJ, grapling, boxing, muy tai or etc... it's already an important edge against average agressor in a street fight.

Why I personally choose BJJ, because it have grappling base, and after first trainings you understand how much you're not feeling your body, how much untrained person is not in control, not even avare of his body. And BJJ helps me be in my body, feel all my muscles, control it. And that what really might be helpful.

Second thing is that it really teaches you to think strategicly, think of every move, yes most of the time you think in terms of BJJ rules, but the idea and habit of calmly think of the next most effective move easily can be applied in a street fight too. In life generally!

And the third, IMHO BJJ is much more sustainable martial art against Boxing or raw grappling in a perspective: when you are a middle aged man, have family, bussiness, kids... you don't necessarily prioritize being champion, you don't have such body recovering ability as young guys, but you want to be strong, you want to be able to fight. And BJJ alows you to do so even when you get old. Yes if you are young, you can easily be explosive and agressive BJJ fighter, but you can be still competitive and effective in BJJ even when you not. I believe in many other martial arts you have  a much less time to do this sports effectively, and after that you will be getting more injures and less fun, than actually training and improving.

But that's just my perspective.

text:
It didn't matter how muscular and strong I got in the gym, or the sports I played... It wasn't until I trained in how to fight -  and also the experience of getting in a few fights (but I never picked a fight).  It even helps to feel what it is like to be punched in the face a few times... It was only then did I finally realize what fight training could mean to certain people. For me it was true, down to the core, confidence, and I mean in how it reaches out to all areas of one's life.
My suggestion for people who want to learn some basic self defence, is the old belief (that I am going to totally butcher now) which is... do not to try and learn every of the 1000's of defensive and offensive moves, but take two or three moves and practice those skills 1000's of times over and over.  
One side note ... no matter how great this art is... you still need to learn how to throw a few good punches, especially in a bar fight.

text:
Martial arts will absolutely work in the street, if you train them with proper intent. If you are a sport grappler, then the video is right, a street fight probably won't go well for you. If you train whatever style you are learning with intent to protect yourself, then you will likely be fine. Of course, there are no guarantees, but based on my experience, this statement is true. 

BJJ as commonly taught today, is not conducive to a real world situation, because it primarily only focuses on the ground fighting techniques... you know, literally the last place you want to be in the real world. While that is good to know, it is more than likely that you will respond based on how you train, and typically at the lowest level of your training. So get out there and train with intent, and bring back what martial arts were for, being martial.

text:
I know how powerful BJJ is because I train MMA, but for me this is not a "real" test. The kickboxer and the boxer couldn't strike as hard as if it was a real fight. This is important because if the BJJ guy feels danger when he tries to shorten distance, he will have more dificulties to execute the takedown. Meanwhile, the BJJ guy could go as hard as he wants on the floor because it is not so harmful as punches and kicks. On the other hand, the kickboxer didn't throw a lot of punches-kick combos, which should be his advantage (specially low kicks), and the two of them were too near of the BJJ guy without throwing. As my master (BJJ and Luta Livre black belt) says: BJJ and LV are great but in a MMA fight, when you get hit hard, it all changes.

I know the intention of the video and it's great :) but I hate when people without fighting experiencie make comments like "see, BJJ always wins, BJJ is the best martial art for the streets" by watching this type of videos haha

text:
Good choice of style comparison. The boxer threw some very heavy and quick punches. Once the BJJ guy closed the distance and realised single legs were a bad idea he got better. 
I think he would have secured a submission for sure eventually, although i think boxer did tap once towards end?  ( i might be mistaken!)

The boxer’s speed made the BJJ fighter hesitate to commit to any lock as quickly as a more experienced BJJ practitioner might have. 

Overall, it was a good contest, and I think I’d call it a draw based on what we saw. The BJJ guy has an extremely good chin, though! 

To be completely fair, if the boxer had MMA gloves, he could have seriously damaged the BJJ fighter, particularly during those rapid punch flurries and when BJJ took him to the ground and allowed him some time to move. 

Hard to test in a dojo safely, but if the boxer had been wearing MMA gloves, the BJJ guy might have been knocked unconscious or I imagine suffered broken ribs on his left side within the first 30 to 40 seconds.  Having been punched myself by a decent boxer who was wearing MMA gloves I can testify to the rib thing lol 

Great video as always, your channel is really what some more established channels should have been doing, you guys should be proud. Fare play to both fighters and your team as a whole.

В свою чергу, якщо він буде одягнений у вбрання з довгим рукавом, борець буде мати додаткову фору для захватів, особливо для самбістів та борців дзю-до. Тут вага навпаки в мінус боксеру, хоча Нікіта добре всаджував двійки та комбінації в суперника. Можливо трішки легший боксер був би більш прудкий і верткий, але Нікіта вправно використовував дистанцію та  діяв обачливо. Не забуваємо, що вулиця - це не тільки руки, а і ноги, і лікті. На додачу, хлопці цілком атлетичні, контролюють дихалку та уміло виходять з кризових для себе ситуацій, що допомогло Русіку загалом "вціліти" у поєдинку, завдяки витривалості. text:
It is also worth mentioning that BJJ is great but for controlled situations. Situations where you know no one else is joining the fight. You don't want to fight two guys while being on the floor. Also in situations where you are 100% sure that the other guy doesn't have a hidden knife in his pocket because if you try to grapple someone with a knife, you're dead. People say 90% of fights end on the ground but forget that about 100% start in standing positions. So BJJ is the best thing you can use in 1v1 situations while boxing is great if you facing more than one opponent: you can strike one and still be able to run away, while being on the ground you cannot run.
So in situations where you do not control everything arround you better use boxing or muay thai/Kickboxing in order to stay standing a be able to run away or use a martial art that grounds the opponent but keeps you standing like Wrestling or Judo.

text: I've been rather consistently doing some form of martial arts from around the age of 3. My dad started us boxing, then karate, but always boxing (especially sparring). I eventually moved into Muay Thai, Jiu Jitsu and MMA. I still believe that the best thing for self defense is the basics of jiu jitsu or wrestling, to create space and get up if someone pins you and then... long distance running. Self defense is not about beating the person in front of you, but getting away safely. If you are standing and the person in front of you doesn't have a hold of you, turn and run. If your ego gets in the way and you want to fight and beat the person in front you, that's another question all together and you might want to start looking at yourself and your situational awareness. Self defense should never be about engaging, but rather disengaging and getting away SAFELY.

text: In my late 50s now and can speak with a great deal of personal experience having been in many street fights, bar brawls, etc. Also, very experienced in what I consider the best base a person can have for self defense at the time I trained. Before I list them I want to make it clear, there is a HUGE difference in self-defense and prepared fighting. When two people are prepared to fight one another there no longer exist an element of surprise. The element of surprise is a big plus. Self-defense is based on surprise and trying everything possible to actually avoid conflicts, and in almost all cases anyone who is highly trained usually embraces the practice of avoiding conflicts. With all that said, this is what I was successful in and trained heavily in for many years. Folkstyle wrestling, boxing, WKA Kickboxing (not US PKA), and a touch of JKD (wasn't much of that around in 80s). Training in all these styles one of the best things I learned was proper distance and timing, you'll be surprised how effective just not getting hit or being taken down can be🤣. The other thing is you gain a sense of calm, if you're constantly training in combat with other high level people a street confrontation doesn't concern you, unless you're confronted by multiple attackers and you're by yourself. Bit older now and would like to try some BJJ, that wasn't around when I was younger. One last thing I will say that makes a big difference is one's will. So whatever you train in, train hard, and try to avoid confrontations. But if the confrontation cannot be avoided, believe in yourself, don't give up, and if you overwhelm your attacker don't over do it.

text:
It great to see Tony Jeffries experiencing something new and sharing his experiences from the perspective of a beginner.  

It's also refreshing to hear a YouTube influencer with professional fighting experience state that, yes, training does count towards being able to defend yourself.  It has become the trend for some influential  martial arts YouTubers to totally dismiss sport fighting and martial arts - even the pragmatic ones like MMA, boxing, and BJJ calling them sports and ill equipped for actual self-defence.  In fact, one well known martial arts YouTuber, who is a former professional MMA fighter, who I respect, boldly states: "Most martial artists don't know how to fight."  I do agree that some fighting arts are more suited to give you self-defence skills while others are not. 

That said, I would say that both boxing and BJJ (or other grappling art) are useful for self-defence for different purposes.   

Boxing (as well as kickboxing, and muay Thai) not only teaches you how to strike a moving target and evading strikes, but it also trains you the conditioning to absorb hits.  No one wants to take a hit, not even in a light semi-contact spar, but boxing (and kickboxing, muay Thai, and some of the harder karate styles) will train that mental focus to not fold under pressure of getting punched.  This is where untrained fighters fall apart is when they get hit for real the first time and go into a confused state of shock and panic -- especially if you get cut or bleed.  

There is that argument that you want to stay on your feet in a self-defence situation because there might be multiple attackers although I think that's often overblown because most attacks - unless you frequent rough bars or neighborhoods - are probably more 1-on-1 like a road rage incident, or some street person with mental health issues attacking you.  

The one valid argument for not taking someone to the ground is that there are no comfy mats on the street to fall on.  Example: during an MMA class I was taking one time we were doing take take down drills.   I was a three striped BJJ blue belt at the time and my opponent for the shark tank drill was a beginner.  I easily got a single leg but my head was out of position to his outside and he instinctively guillotined my head by instinct as I drove him to the mat and my head got spiked ("DDT" in professional wrestling circles).  While I was okay due to the mat and my excessively hard head the situation may have been a different outcome if it were on concrete.

Now although one can argue that you can do a safer standing throw like a seoi nage, uchi-mata, or kosoto gari, you are unlikely to use those techniques due to their low probability unless you are a black belt in judo.  As a BJJ guy you are unlikely to be really, really good at those throws especially because the first two expose your back so you're unlikely to train them regularly and so a typical BJJ guy is unlikely to be as well versed with standing throws as a judo brown or black belt especially since the attacker is unlikely to be wearing a do-gi.  The BJJ bread and butter is likely to be a double leg, and single leg and those moves entail some risk because you are driving the opponent to the ground and going with him on to hard concrete.

However BJJ is relevant if the conditions are right, and especially if the attacker happens to be wearing a Golden Gloves Champion T-shirt!  BJJ has it's benefits against a single attacker; especially if they are more aggressive than you.  If you can clinch up and even take them to the ground they are unlikely to be able to throw any kind of meaningful punches.  BJJ is also a more humane way of dealing with a single attacker as video footage of Ryan Hall, and Matt Serra subduing aggressors in a restaurant and holding them -- again, evidence that many attacks in daily life are likely to be 1-on-1 than the worst case multiple attackers in a bar scenario -- unless you happen to be in a bar.   Also, what if you're getting overwhelmed by punches?  What do MMA fighters automatically do when they are getting overwhelmed with punches -- they will go for a double leg or other takedown to try and survive.

The one argument I use against those you say that ground grappling is pointless for street self-defence because they would never take the fight to the ground is: what if you get taken to the ground?  Every punk who watches UFC has seen a double-leg and probably tried it on a friend while roughhousing.  If you get taken to the ground do you know how to escape?  Do you know how to bridge escape if you get mounted?  Do you know how to do a technical standup so you don't get kicked in the face while scrambling up?

One martial art that has not been mentioned as very good for self-defence is muay Thai.  Muay Thai addresses multiple ranges.  Although it lacks the ground game, it addresses kicking range, punching range, knee and elbow range, and clinching range.  It has the strikes using 8 limbs, it has the conditioning to keep you physically fit, it has taken clinching and elevated it to a specialized set of skills, and has very effective trips throws from the clinch and you do not need sleeves or lapels to do them. 

But if I had to choose between boxing and BJJ for street self-defence...hmmmmm...tough choice because they are both important.  But for me I'm going to say BJJ specifically designed for self-defence (e.g. Gracie Combatives).  No fancy worm guards, no lasso grips or berimbolos,...just dealing with an aggressive unskilled attacker throwing haymakers.

Of course, there's the other option: stay out of trouble, don't piss other people off, learn to keep the ego in check and walk away...run if you must because a street attack is no about winning; it's about making sure no one gets seriously hurt especially you.

text:
Somethings to think about for self protection in an unarmed "street confrontation", especially if you're by yourself.

If they are throwing strikes at you, you are usually at a distance where you can break away and run. If they grab you, you now have to deal with the grab/hold first before you can break away and run.

Also with grappling, if someone takes you down in the street, you have a better idea of how to get back to your feet.

And some old school Gracie Jiu Jitsu schools still do sparring with punches. One of the common strategies is to put up a high shield and ram into the puncher and enter into a clinch to a takedown.

text:
Tony
Love your boxing videos.

I personally think that Bjj is not a very practical art for self defense particularly in a street fight scenario where the surface is hard concrete, uneven, scattered with broken glass, stones etc.
Getting your opponent to the ground with the hope of securing an armbar, triangle or RNC  will get you injured before you do any damage to your adversary due to the surface you are fighting on.

The practical aspects of Bjj for the street would be, knowing how to fall (breakfall),  takedown defense, defense against a standing a choke, but these can be learnt from wrestling with the exception of choke defense.
So I would say boxing with some good takedown defense and maybe the ability to take someone down is mostly what you need.
In the ring or on the mat is a different story, where a grappling art will likely prevail most of the time.
Just my 2 cents.

text: One thing about the ground that I believe goes unmentioned many times is that if you end up on the ground it could be because you were already tackled, kicked or hit or taken down in such a way that you broke something and can no longer defend yourself effectively on the ground even if you know jiu-jitsu. So even for a jiu-jitsu practitioner he may be in a disadvantageous situation by the time he is on the ground; he could twist something in the clinch as well. Boxing helps to get away from the situation before an injury leading the person to the ground happens. Also what most people today seem to not discuss very much is the clinch where a lot of grappling happens and which is the transitional range between boxing and the ground. If the defender in the clinch has judo or other clinch grappling skill he might be relatively comfortable in that range where the opponent presumably believed himself to be superior, probably based on his size. So even in a grappling scenario the ground does not just happen right away when the boxing range is closed but rather the situation must first pass through the clinch unless one person was tackled or knocked down by a strike.

Never done boxing, but heres my hot take on BJJ as a purple belt. You can do every single NoGi move in the Gi, but not vice versa. text: boxing cons in the street: taken down easily, injure hand especially if power punching to the head, and takes too long to end the fight unless you land a lucky KO shot. these are just too many variables to be worrying about in the middle of a fight. on the other hand, grappling teaches you how to take them down which stops them from striking, and you can choose how to end the fight (control or submission). cons of grappling is when you're on the ground its easy for someone to stomp you out, and sometimes the opponent is too heavy or strong so you have to resort to using more leverage techniques which can be difficult to perform. its also easier to pair grappling with weapons than it is to pair boxing with weapons (grappling allows disarms and limb control while boxing doesnt do either)
